title: Observation of a power transfer controlled by the phase of a quantum superposition
authors: Nathanaël Cottet, Sébastien Jezouin, Bogdan Reznychenko, Alexia Auffèves, Benjamin Huard
abstract: A driven qubit exchanges energy with the propagating modes that drive it. When two spatially separated modes drive a single qubit with opposite amplitudes, their net action on the qubit cancels. Yet the qubit can still transfer power from one mode to the other through stimulated emission. The directionality originates from opposite stimulated emission powers into each line. We realize this situation with a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two transmission lines and show that the direction of the power flow is set by the phase $φ$ of the qubit superposition between its ground and excited states, rather than by any classical control parameter. From a time-resolved measurement of the output power in one line, we observe a transfer that varies as $\cosφ$ and hence changes direction between $φ=0$ and $φ=π$. The directionality of the total power flow is limited by the phase independent contributions of the reflected drive and of spontaneous emission, which sets a routing efficiency that we measure as a function of the input power. For an equal superposition of ground and excited qubit states (maximal coherence), the efficiency reaches $63\%$, close to the bound of $69\%$ expected from the measured qubit coherence times.
summary: The researchers demonstrated that a superconducting transmon qubit can transfer power directionally between two microwave transmission lines based solely on the relative phase ($\phi$) of its superposition state. By setting opposing input drives, they showed the output power oscillates as $\cos(\phi)$, proving that quantum coherence dictates the energy routing in this open quantum system.
main_problem: To determine if the direction of energy flow (power transfer) between two spatially separated electromagnetic modes driven by a single qubit can be controlled by the quantum phase ($\phi$) of the qubit's superposition state.
main_result: The power transfer exhibits a clear, continuous transition in direction as $\phi$ changes, following a $\cos(\phi)$ dependence. This directional pumping is fundamentally controlled by the qubit's coherence rather than classical drive parameters.
method: Time-resolved measurement of output photon flux in one transmission line while applying opposite-amplitude drives to two coupled lines.
model_or_system: The system uses a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two microwave transmission lines. The dynamics are analyzed using input-output relations derived from the Hamiltonian, focusing on stimulated emission competing with reflected drive and spontaneous emission.
key_observables: Output power in one line ($\langle a_{	ext{out}}^\dagger a_{	ext{out}}angle$), photon routing efficiency ($\eta$), and the dependence of transfer amplitude on $\cos(\phi)$.
important_parameters: The phase $\phi$ of the qubit superposition, the coherence parameter $\langle\sigma_xangle$, and the ratio between spontaneous vs. stimulated emission rates.
main_assumptions: The directionality is limited by phase-independent contributions from reflected drive and spontaneous emission; the analysis assumes a lossless emitter coupled to the lines.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup showing power transfer driven by two lines, demonstrating that when drives cancel, power transfers via coherence ($\propto \langle\sigma_xangle$). A key figure shows the output power varying as $\cos(\phi)$, confirming directionality switching.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (qubit coupled to two lines), derives the outgoing photon flux equations, and then analyzes the directional transfer by setting input drives to cancel ($\Omega_a = -\Omega_b$), showing the dependence on $\cos(\phi)$ through time-resolved measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean demonstration of quantum control over energy flow in an open quantum system (qubit coupled to waveguides), directly linking directional photon emission to the phase coherence ($\phi$) of the emitter, which is central to understanding quantum thermodynamics and measurement processes.
